prompt: What is a React component, fundamentally?
choices: A class that extends `HTMLElement`.
A JavaScript function that takes a props object and returns a tree of React elements (JSX).
A template string with interpolation.
A subclass of the DOM.

prompt: Why must React components be capitalized (`<Button>` not `<button>`)?
choices: It is a stylistic preference enforced by ESLint.
JSX uses capitalization to distinguish components from native DOM elements.
Only capitalized tags can have children.
It avoids reserved-word collisions in TypeScript.

prompt: After calling `setCount(count + 1)`, can you read the new value of `count` synchronously in the same function?
choices: Yes — state updates are synchronous.
No — state updates are batched and applied between renders, so the new value is only visible after the next render.
Only if you call `setCount` twice.
Only inside an effect.

prompt: Why prefer the function form `setCount(c => c + 1)` over `setCount(count + 1)` when updating state from async handlers?
choices: It is shorter.
It avoids stale-closure bugs by always operating on the latest committed state.
It is the only form supported in React 19.
It bypasses re-rendering.

prompt: What does an empty dependency array `useEffect(() => { ... }, [])` mean?
choices: Run the effect after every render.
Run the effect once after the initial render, then never again.
Run only on unmount.
Disable the effect entirely.

prompt: When should `useEffect` NOT be your first reach?
choices: When fetching data.
When the work can happen directly in an event handler (a button click or form submit).
When subscribing to a websocket.
When integrating with a non-React DOM library.

prompt: Why is using the array index as the `key` in a list usually a bug?
choices: Indexes are non-deterministic.
When items are reordered, inserted, or deleted, React mismatches DOM nodes to data, causing state to leak between rows and animations to target the wrong elements.
Indexes are not allowed in JSX.
Indexes are slower than strings.

prompt: What is a 'controlled' input in React?
choices: An input wrapped in a Context Provider.
An input whose current value is held in React state and updated through `onChange`.
A read-only input.
An input that uses `defaultValue` instead of `value`.

prompt: When is `useReducer` typically a better choice than `useState`?
choices: When the component is a class.
When state has multiple sub-values that update together, or when transitions deserve named actions for debuggability.
When fetching data.
When using TypeScript.

prompt: What does `useMemo` do, and when does it actually help?
choices: It memoizes any function automatically.
It caches a computed value between renders; it helps when the computation is genuinely expensive (large lists, heavy math) — sprinkling it everywhere wastes effort.
It re-runs the function on every render.
It replaces `useState` for object values.

prompt: Why can a single 'app state' Context become a performance trap?
choices: Context can't hold objects.
Every consumer re-renders when the context value changes by reference, so combining unrelated state in one context causes cascading re-renders.
Context disables state updates.
Context only works at the root.

prompt: What is the right first step when a React app feels slow?
choices: Wrap every component in `React.memo`.
Use the React DevTools Profiler to identify which components are rendering and why before guessing.
Switch to a different framework.
Disable strict mode.
